blocks.text: MCP’s architecture is built from just three roles, host, client, and server, connected by a message-passing conversation that always follows the same basic shape.

This lesson is a wide-angle map of that structure, enough to see how the pieces fit together, before later modules zoom into each piece individually, MCP Fundamentals for definitions, MCP Architecture the module for a much deeper structural dive, and Building MCP Servers and Building MCP Clients for hands-on implementation.
1. The Host: Where a Person Actually Is

blocks.alt: A user interacts with the host
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785439735790-260350203.png

The host is the application a real person opens and interacts with, a chat interface, a code editor, a voice assistant. The host is responsible for the overall user experience, and for deciding which MCP servers it wants to connect to on the user’s behalf.

A single host can, and very often does, maintain connections to several different servers at once, a coding assistant host might connect to a file-system server, a terminal server, and a version-control server, all simultaneously.

blocks.title: A quick self-check
blocks.content: If you can point to the specific window or app a user has open, you have found the host, everything else, client and server, is invisible plumbing behind it.

blocks.text: Popular examples of hosts today include AI-enabled code editors, desktop chat assistants, and increasingly, backend services that run AI agents without any visible user interface at all, the host role does not strictly require a graphical window, just the overall orchestrating application.

Whatever form the host takes, its defining trait is the same, it is the thing ultimately accountable for what the user experiences, everything else in this architecture exists to serve that one application.
2. The Client: The Protocol Speaker Living Inside the Host

blocks.alt: A host runs a client that speaks the MCP protocol
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785439735790-675013781.png

The client is a piece of code, usually a small library, that lives inside the host and does the actual work of speaking MCP, sending requests, waiting for responses, tracking the state of an ongoing session. Critically, a client maintains a one-to-one connection with exactly one server, if a host needs to talk to three servers, it runs three separate client instances, one per server, each with its own independent connection and state.

It helps to think of the client as a translator standing between the host’s general-purpose code and one specific server’s particular protocol conversation, the host asks in general terms, the client translates that into precise MCP messages.

code.content:
# a host managing three separate client instances
file_client = MCPClient(server="file-system-server")
calendar_client = MCPClient(server="calendar-server")
search_client = MCPClient(server="web-search-server")

blocks.text: Client libraries exist in several languages, and a host developer typically just imports one rather than implementing the low-level message handling by hand, in much the same way a web developer imports an HTTP client rather than writing raw socket code.
3. The Server: Where the Real Capability Lives

blocks.alt: A client connects to a server, which holds the real capability
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785439735791-971009623.png

The server is a separate program that actually implements tools, resources, and prompts, usually by wrapping some existing system, a file system, a database, a third-party API. A server has no idea what host or client is talking to it beyond what the protocol tells it, this deliberate ignorance is a feature, not a limitation, it is exactly what lets one server be reused by many different hosts without any special-casing.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Role","Lives where","Responsible for"],"rows":[["Host","The application a user opens","Overall experience, deciding which servers to connect to"],["Client","Inside the host, one per server","Speaking MCP, managing one connection"],["Server","A separate program","Exposing tools, resources, and prompts"]]}

blocks.text: A single server can be, and often is, used by many different hosts simultaneously, a popular open-source file-system server might be running unmodified inside dozens of unrelated chat applications and coding tools at once.

blocks.title: A useful comparison
blocks.content: A well-built MCP server is a bit like a well-built library in any programming language, it does one thing well, documents itself clearly, and has no idea, and no need to know, who its eventual caller will be.

blocks.text: This lack of assumptions about the caller is exactly what allowed community-built servers to spring up so quickly once MCP launched, an author could build a genuinely useful server without needing to coordinate with every possible host application in advance.

blocks.title: One more angle on this
blocks.content: A server author generally writes it once and never has to think about which specific chat app, coding tool, or voice assistant will eventually connect to it, that decoupling is the whole point.

blocks.text: 4. The Connection Between Client and Server

A client and server communicate over a transport, the actual pipe messages travel through, which might be standard input and output for a locally running server, or an HTTP-based connection for a remote one. Regardless of which transport is used, the messages themselves follow the same format, JSON-RPC, covered in full in the MCP Communication Protocol module, so the client’s logic for interpreting a response does not need to change depending on which transport carried it.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Transport","Typical use case"],"rows":[["STDIO","A locally running server, launched as a subprocess"],["HTTP-based","A remote server, reachable over the network"]]}

blocks.text: Choosing between these transports, covered in full in the dedicated Transport Mechanisms module, usually comes down to one simple question, is the server running on the same machine as the host, or somewhere else entirely.

It is worth noting that switching a server from one transport to another, say from STDIO to an HTTP-based remote deployment, does not usually require changing the tool logic inside the server itself, only how the messages travel in and out.

Whichever transport is chosen, the client code calling list_tools or call_tool looks identical, the transport is an implementation detail the rest of the host application does not usually need to think about at all.
5. The Request-Response Flow, Step by Step

blocks.alt: A client sends a request to the server, which sends back a response
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785439735791-320589068.png
A typical exchange looks like this: the client sends a request, a JSON message asking the server to do something, like listing its tools or calling a specific one.
The server processes that request and sends back a response, another JSON message, containing either a result or an error.

This is fundamentally the same request-response pattern used across countless other systems, MCP’s contribution is standardizing exactly what these requests and responses look like for AI tool use specifically.

Every request carries a unique id, which the matching response echoes back, this is what lets a client correctly match an incoming response to the specific request it originally sent, even if several requests are in flight at once.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Field","Purpose"],"rows":[["jsonrpc","Marks the message as following the JSON-RPC format"],["id","Uniquely matches a response back to its request"],["method","Which operation is being requested, like tools/call"]]}

blocks.text: 6. Initialization: How a Session Actually Begins

blocks.alt: A client initializes, beginning the session
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785439736193-526676675.png

Before any tool gets called, a client and server go through an initialization handshake, the client announces itself and what it supports, the server responds with its own supported capabilities, and both sides agree on a shared protocol version. Only after this handshake completes does the connection become a fully usable session, this upfront negotiation is what prevents a client from accidentally trying to use a feature the server does not actually support.
This handshake typically happens automatically, hidden inside whatever MCP client library a host is using, an application developer rarely needs to hand-write the initialization messages themselves.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Who sends it"],"rows":[["Initialize request","Client, announcing its own supported capabilities"],["Initialize response","Server, announcing its supported capabilities back"],["Initialized notification","Client, confirming the session is ready to use"]]}

code.content:
# a simplified initialization exchange
client.send({"method": "initialize", "params": {"protocolVersion": "2025-06-18"}})
server_response = client.receive()
client.send({"method": "notifications/initialized"})

blocks.text: If either side tries to skip this handshake, most well-behaved client and server implementations will simply refuse to proceed, treating an un-initialized session as not yet ready for any real tool or resource requests.
7. Capabilities: What Each Side Actually Offers

Not every server implements every part of the protocol, one server might only offer tools, another might offer tools and resources but no prompts. Capabilities are how each side communicates exactly what it supports during initialization, letting a client adjust its behavior accordingly, for example, not bothering to ask a server for prompts if that server already declared it does not support them.

Capability negotiation is deliberately explicit rather than assumed, a client should never simply try calling a resources-related method and hope for the best, it should check the negotiated capabilities first.

This negotiation step is also forward-compatible by design, a newer client talking to an older server will simply see fewer capabilities declared, and can gracefully avoid using features the older server does not yet support.

code.content:
# a rough shape of a server's declared capabilities
{"capabilities": {"tools": {}, "resources": {"subscribe": True}}}

blocks.content: {"headers":["Capability","What declaring it means"],"rows":[["tools","The server can list and execute callable actions"],["resources","The server can list and provide readable context"],["prompts","The server can list and supply reusable templates"]]}

blocks.text: A client that skips checking capabilities and simply guesses what a server supports risks sending a request the server has no handler for, resulting in an avoidable protocol-level error rather than a clean, expected response.
8. Multiple Servers, One Host, Many Independent Clients

blocks.alt: A host runs client 1 and client 2, each connecting to its own server
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785439736194-17651416.png

Because each client manages exactly one connection, a host juggling several servers is really just running several clients side by side, each with its own session, its own capabilities, and its own independent lifecycle. If one server’s connection drops, it does not affect the others, this isolation is a direct architectural consequence of the one-client-per-server design.

This isolation also has a practical security benefit, a compromised or misbehaving server cannot directly interfere with a completely separate client’s connection to a different server, each connection is its own contained relationship.

code.content:
# each client tracks its own session independently
file_client.session.is_active     # True
calendar_client.session.is_active # True, entirely independent of file_client

blocks.text: This per-connection independence is also why adding a brand-new server to an existing host is usually a low-risk change, the new client and its session are additive, they do not touch the wiring of any client already running.
9. Stateless Servers, Stateful Sessions

blocks.alt: A stateless server is compared against a stateful session
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785439736195-314549306.png

Many MCP servers are designed to be stateless in themselves, each tool call is handled independently, with no memory of previous calls baked into the server’s own logic. What does carry state across calls is the session, the ongoing connection tracked by the client, this separation keeps servers simple to write and easy to scale, while the client and host layer handle whatever conversation-level memory is actually needed.

This design mirrors a broader pattern seen across much of distributed systems engineering, keeping the units that do actual work, servers, simple and stateless, while pushing state management to a layer specifically designed to handle it, the session.

blocks.title: Why this matters at scale
blocks.content: Stateless servers are far easier to run multiple copies of behind a load balancer, since any copy can handle any incoming request, a benefit explored fully in the Production MCP module.

blocks.text: This does not mean a server can never remember anything at all, a server can still persist data to its own underlying database, it just means the server does not typically rely on remembering details about the specific ongoing MCP conversation itself.
10. How Errors Propagate Back Through the Layers

When something goes wrong inside a server, that failure has to travel back up through the same three layers it came through, the server returns a structured error to the client, the client surfaces that error to the host, and the host decides what to do with it, retry, show the user a message, or let the AI model attempt to recover by rephrasing its request.

items: Server detects a problem, invalid input, a failed downstream call, or an internal fault.
Server sends back a structured error response instead of a normal result.
Client receives the error and passes it upward to the host.
Host decides how to respond, silently retrying, informing the user, or letting the model try a different approach.

blocks.text: This layered propagation also means a host can apply consistent, application-wide error handling policies, like automatically retrying a timeout once, without needing to special-case that logic separately for every different server it happens to be connected to.
11. Where the AI Model Actually Fits In

It is worth being explicit here: the AI model itself is not one of the three MCP roles, the model lives inside, or alongside, the host, and it is the host’s job to take the model’s intentions, "I want to check the weather," and turn them into an actual client call to the right server. The model never talks to a server directly, it always goes through the host and its client.

This indirection is a deliberate design choice, it means the model’s only real job is deciding what it wants to do, expressed in natural language or a structured function-call format, while all the actual MCP mechanics stay entirely the host and client’s responsibility.

blocks.title: A helpful phrase to remember
blocks.content: The model proposes, the host and client dispose, the model decides what it wants to happen, the surrounding MCP machinery is responsible for actually making it happen safely and correctly.

blocks.text: This also means a single model could, in principle, be swapped out for a different one entirely without the client-server architecture underneath needing any changes, reinforcing the portability benefit covered in the Why MCP lesson.
12. A Worked Example: Three Roles in One Scenario

A user opens a chat app, the host, and asks it to summarize a document. The chat app’s file-reading client connects to a file-system server, requests the document, resource, and receives its content back. The chat app then feeds that content to its AI model, which produces a summary shown to the user. Three roles, one clean flow, host orchestrating, client speaking the protocol, server providing the actual capability.

Notice that if the same chat app later wants to also let the model send an email summarizing the document, that just means adding a second client, connected to an email server, running alongside the first, the file-system client keeps working completely unchanged.

code.content:
# roughly what the host orchestrates
doc = file_client.read_resource("file:///report.txt")
summary = ai_model.summarize(doc)
show_to_user(summary)

blocks.title: Zoom out for a second
blocks.content: Every additional capability added later in this curriculum, tools, resources, prompts, notifications, plugs into this exact same three-role picture, nothing about the fundamental shape changes as more features are layered on.

blocks.text: 13. Common Mistakes When Learning MCP Architecture

items: Confusing host and client, remember the host is the whole application, the client is the specific internal piece managing one server connection.
Assuming a client can talk to multiple servers at once, each client instance manages exactly one connection, a host wanting multiple servers runs multiple clients.
Forgetting the initialization handshake exists, and being surprised when a tool call fails because capabilities were never negotiated first.
Thinking the AI model talks to servers directly, it always goes through the host and its client, the model never holds an MCP connection itself.

blocks.text: A fifth common mistake is assuming a server needs to know anything about the host or model calling it, a well-designed server stays deliberately generic, unaware of and indifferent to whichever specific application happens to be connected.

A sixth common mistake is assuming that every part of the protocol is mandatory for every server, in reality a very simple server might only implement tools and skip resources and prompts entirely, and that is a perfectly valid, complete MCP server.

A seventh common mistake is assuming architecture diagrams like the one at the top of this lesson describe a fixed, rigid pipeline, in practice a host can add or remove client connections dynamically while it is running, the architecture is flexible by design.

An eighth common mistake is expecting a server to reject connections from unfamiliar hosts by default, unless a server author explicitly adds that kind of restriction, most MCP servers will happily accept a connection from any correctly speaking client.
14. Practice: Diagram Your Own MCP Setup

Pick an AI application idea, real or hypothetical, that needs to use two or three different tools. Sketch out which piece is the host, how many client instances it would need, and what each corresponding server would be responsible for, then walk through the initialization handshake for just one of those connections.

code.content:
host = "Research Assistant App"
servers_needed = ["web_search_server", "notes_server"]
clients_needed = len(servers_needed)   # one client instance per server
print(host, "needs", clients_needed, "client instances")

blocks.text: As a further step, sketch what the initialization handshake would look like for the notes_server specifically, what capabilities would it plausibly declare, and what would the client need to check before trying to call one of its tools.

Try also sketching what would need to change if the same host later wanted to support two different web-search servers side by side, notice that this is simply a matter of running a second search client, nothing about the existing architecture needs to be redesigned.

blocks.title: One more thing to try
blocks.content: Consider what would happen architecturally if the notes_server needed to notify the host proactively, without being asked, that a note had changed, this exact scenario is covered by notifications, introduced in the MCP Communication Protocol module next.

blocks.text: Key Takeaway

MCP’s architecture rests on three cleanly separated roles, a host that owns the user experience, one client per server connection doing the actual protocol speaking, and independent servers exposing tools, resources, and prompts, all connected through an initialization handshake and a consistent request-response message flow.

This lesson is the map, the next lesson, MCP Workflow, walks through a full end-to-end conversation in more procedural detail, before MCP Terminology locks down the exact vocabulary this whole curriculum builds on going forward.

Keep the host, client, and server triangle from this lesson firmly in mind, nearly every concept introduced in the rest of this curriculum, sessions, capabilities, transports, tools, resources, prompts, is really just adding detail to one specific corner of this same three-part structure.
